title: Divus Augustus (Life of Augustus), in De Vita Caesarum (The Twelve Caesars)
author: Suetonius
citation_detail: Loeb Classical Library 31. Trans. J. C. Rolfe. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1914 (revised 1998). Key chapters: ch. 5 (birth, 23 September 63 BCE); ch. 7–8 (adoption by Caesar, names); ch. 79 (physical appearance); ch. 99–100 (death and last words, 19 August 14 CE). Full Life of Augustus runs chs. 1–101.
note: Closest extant biography; includes personal details, appearance, character, death scene. Written c. 121 CE by imperial secretary with access to archives. LCL 31 (Rolfe 1914, rev. 1998). Reliability: A (anecdotal details reliable; interpretation and gossip require caution).
bibliographic_hint: Suetonius. "Divus Augustus" (Life of Augustus), in De Vita Caesarum (The Twelve Caesars). Written c. 120 CE.

title: Roman History, Books 45–56
author: Cassius Dio
citation_detail: Loeb Classical Library: LCL 66 (Books 41–45, Cary 1916), LCL 82 (Books 46–50, Cary 1917), LCL 83 (Books 51–55, Cary 1917), LCL 175 (Book 56–60, Cary 1924). Cambridge: Harvard University Press. Books 45–56 cover Octavian/Augustus from Caesar's death (44 BCE) to Augustus's death (14 CE). Book 53 covers constitutional settlements of 27 BCE and 23 BCE in detail.
note: Most detailed continuous narrative of Augustus's career. LCL 66, 82, 83, 175 (Cary 1916–1924). Reliability: A (comprehensive but written 150+ years after events; sometimes conflates traditions; primary source for constitutional settlements).
bibliographic_hint: Cassius Dio. Roman History, Books 45–56. Written c. 200–230 CE.

title: Bella Civilia (Civil Wars), Books 3–5
author: Appian
citation_detail: Loeb Classical Library 543–544. Trans. Brian McGing. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2020. (Older edition: LCL 3–5, trans. Horace White, 1913.) Books 3–4: Second Triumvirate, proscriptions (43 BCE), Philippi (42 BCE). Book 5: war against Sextus Pompeius (38–36 BCE) and dissolution of Triumvirate.
note: Key source for Second Triumvirate period, proscriptions, war against Sextus Pompeius. LCL 543–544 (McGing 2020). Reliability: A (detailed military narrative; corroborate political interpretations with Dio and Suetonius).
bibliographic_hint: Appian. Bella Civilia (Civil Wars), Books 3–5. Written mid-2nd century CE.

title: Res Gestae Divi Augusti
author: Augustus (Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus)
citation_detail: Standard scholarly editions: (1) Cooley, Alison E. Res Gestae Divi Augusti: Text, Translation, and Commentary. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009. ISBN 978-0-521-60067-4. (2) Brunt, P. A. and J. M. Moore. Res Gestae Divi Augusti. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1967. No Loeb edition exists. Most complete surviving copy: Monumentum Ancyranum (Ankara, Turkey). Cooley 2009 is the current preferred critical edition.
note: First-person funerary inscription dictated by Augustus. Self-presentation only — NOT neutral history; omits defeats (Teutoburg Forest) and selectively narrates achievements. Reliability: A (primary document for official Augustan claims; rhetorical bias explicitly noted in claims CLM_AU_018 and CLM_AU_027).
bibliographic_hint: Res Gestae Divi Augusti. Composed by Augustus before his death. Most complete copy: Monumentum Ancyranum, Ankara, Turkey.

title: Annales (Annals), Book 1
author: Tacitus
citation_detail: Loeb Classical Library 249. Trans. John Jackson. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1931. Book 1 covers 14–15 CE (Augustus's death and Tiberius's accession). Ann. 1.1–15: retrospective assessment of Augustus's reign; Ann. 1.5–6: Tacitus's account of Livia and Augustus's death.
note: Retrospective assessment of Augustus's death and legacy. LCL 249 (Jackson 1931). Reliability: A (analytical but retrospective; interpretive and skeptical toward the Principate; Ann. 1.5–6 on Livia as hostile tradition, rejected by most modern scholars).
bibliographic_hint: Tacitus. Annales (Annals), Book 1. Written c. 115–120 CE.

title: Life of Antony (Antonius), in Bioi Paralleloi (Parallel Lives)
author: Plutarch
citation_detail: Loeb Classical Library 101. Trans. Bernadotte Perrin. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1920. Covers Octavian-Antony rivalry throughout. Key chapters for Augustan context: ch. 16–22 (Second Triumvirate, proscriptions); ch. 33–36 (Brundisium agreement, 40 BCE); ch. 56–71 (buildup to Actium); ch. 75–77 (Actium, 31 BCE) and aftermath.
note: Covers rivalry between Octavian and Mark Antony. LCL 101 (Perrin 1920). Reliability: A (standard biographical source; moralising narrative; compare with Cassius Dio Books 48–51 for political detail).
bibliographic_hint: Plutarch. "Life of Antony" (Antonius), in Bioi Paralleloi (Parallel Lives). Written c. 100–120 CE.

title: Life of Augustus (Bios Kaisaros)
author: Nicolaus of Damascus
citation_detail: No Loeb Classical Library edition exists. Standard critical edition: Toher, Mark. Nicolaus of Damascus: The Life of Augustus and the Autobiography. Cambridge Classical Texts and Commentaries 53. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2017. ISBN 978-0-521-83777-2. The text survives only in excerpts (Constantinian excerpts); covers Augustus's birth through his early career to c. 31 BCE.
note: Contemporary account by Herod the Great's court historian; Nicolaus knew Augustus personally. Most detailed surviving account of Augustus's early life. Reliability: A (contemporary; but courtly and adulatory perspective; Toher 2017 is the definitive critical edition).
bibliographic_hint: Nicolaus of Damascus. Life of Augustus. Written late 1st century BCE.

title: Roman History (Historia Romana), Book 2
author: Velleius Paterculus
citation_detail: Loeb Classical Library 152. Trans. Frederick W. Shipley. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1924. (Revised edition: trans. A. J. Woodman. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2025.) Book 2, chapters 59–130 cover the period from Caesar's death to the death of Augustus (14 CE). Key chapters: 2.59–61 (Caesar's assassination, Octavian's emergence); 2.86–89 (Actium and aftermath); 2.100–104 (Augustan peace and reforms); 2.123–124 (Tiberius's adoption and succession).
note: Serving military officer under Tiberius; contemporary source for later Augustan period. Strongly pro-Augustan and pro-Tiberian perspective. LCL 152 (Shipley 1924; Woodman 2025 rev.). Reliability: A (contemporary eyewitness for 6–30 CE; bias must be flagged for evaluative claims).
bibliographic_hint: Velleius Paterculus. Roman History. Written c. 30 CE.

title: Philippics; Epistulae ad Atticum (Letters to Atticus)
author: Cicero
citation_detail: Philippics: Loeb Classical Library 189 (Philippics 1–6) and LCL 507 (Philippics 7–14). Trans. D. R. Shackleton Bailey. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2010. Key references for Octavian: Phil. 3.3 (Octavian praised as defender of Republic); Phil. 5.43–44 (Cicero's famous warning about the young Caesar). Epistulae ad Atticum: LCL 7, 8, 200, 201 (4 vols). Trans. D. R. Shackleton Bailey. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1999. Letters of late 44–43 BCE contain frank contemporary assessments of Octavian's emergence.
note: Contemporary political source; Cicero initially allied with Octavian against Antony. Uses name 'Octavianus' (not Caesar). LCL 189, 507 (Philippics); LCL 7, 8, 200, 201 (Letters). Reliability: A (contemporary eyewitness political context; unfiltered primary source for 44–43 BCE).
bibliographic_hint: Cicero. Philippics; Epistulae ad Atticum (Letters to Atticus). 44–43 BCE.

title: The Roman Revolution
author: Ronald Syme
citation_detail: Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1939. Repr. 1960. ISBN 978-0-19-881001-9.
note: Foundational modern work; portrays Augustus as revolutionary who cloaked autocracy in republican language
bibliographic_hint: Syme, Ronald. The Roman Revolution. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1939.

author: Adrian Goldsworthy
citation_detail: New Haven: Yale University Press, 2014. ISBN 978-0-300-17872-5.
note: Modern biography emphasizing that the Principate developed through trial and experimentation
bibliographic_hint: Goldsworthy, Adrian. Augustus: First Emperor of Rome. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2014.
